name: Fibonacci
description: The textbook recursion: F(n) = F(n - 1) + F(n - 2) with F(0) = 0, F(1) = 1. Beautiful to read, exponential to run — and the clearest picture of why memoisation exists.
explanation:
What it is

The recursive Fibonacci implementation translates the mathematical definition almost word for word: two recursive calls, one addition, and base cases that stop the descent. Its call tree is the canonical illustration of overlapping subproblems.

How it works

  1. Base case: n <= 1 returns n.
  2. Recursive case: return F(n - 1) + F(n - 2).
  3. Each call fans out into two — the tree doubles at every level.

Worked example

F(5) calls F(4) and F(3); F(4) calls F(3) and F(2) — F(3) is now being computed twice, and lower values far more often. The total number of calls to compute F(n) is 2 x F(n + 1) - 1, which grows by a factor of about 1.6 per increment of n.

Key insight

The recursion tree contains every subproblem a number of times proportional to its own subtree — the definition of exponential. Adding a memo dictionary (or converting to a bottom-up loop) makes each subproblem run exactly once, collapsing the work from about 1.6^n to n. In production, no version is right: you want the iterative or fast-doubling form; the recursion exists to teach, and to show precisely why DP exists.

use: Teaching recursion and the shape of overlapping subproblems
Call-tree and memoisation visualisations (the difference is dramatic and honest)
Small n (below roughly 30) where the exponential cost is invisible
avoid: n beyond 35-40 — call counts explode by a factor of ~1.6 per step
Anything numeric that runs more than once; memoise or iterate
Deep recursion in languages with small default stacks

commonMistakes.mistake: No memoisation: both recursive branches recompute their entire subtrees, so the same subproblem is solved exponentially many times.
commonMistakes.fix: Cache results in a dict/array keyed by n (or switch to the bottom-up loop), reducing the work from about 1.6^n to n.

commonMistakes.mistake: Imprecise base case: returning n for n <= 1 works only because F(1) = 1; change the sequence definition and the code silently computes a different recurrence.
commonMistakes.fix: State and test the base cases explicitly: F(0) = 0, F(1) = 1, F(2) = 1, F(10) = 55.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming the recursion depth is small because n is small — depth equals n, and n near the interpreter's recursion limit (about 1000 in Python) raises RecursionError even though the tree itself is even more expensive.
commonMistakes.fix: Prefer iteration for large n; raise the recursion limit only as an explicit, documented trade-off.

name: Factorial
description: n! = n x (n - 1) x ... x 1, with 0! = 1. The simplest legitimate recursion: one recursive call per level, no branching, and a clean demonstration of the call stack.
explanation:
What it is

Factorial is the first function most courses use to introduce recursion because it needs none of recursion's subtleties: a single base case, a single recursive call, and a linear chain from n down to 1.

How it works

  1. Base case: n <= 1 returns 1 (covering 0! and 1! at once).
  2. Recursive case: return n * factorial(n - 1).
  3. The calls stack up n deep, then unwind, multiplying on the way back out.

Worked example

factorial(5): the calls descend 5 -> 4 -> 3 -> 2 -> 1, where 1 is returned; unwinding multiplies 2 x 3 x 4 x 5 = 120. The stack held five frames at its deepest — one per level, no more.

Key insight

Time and stack space are both Θ(n), and unlike branching recursions there is nothing to memoise — every subproblem is distinct and used once. The iterative loop is strictly better in space (O(1)) and readability here, which is why factorial is a teaching example rather than a production one. The numbers also grow absurdly fast: 20! is about 2.4 x 10^18 and already past 64-bit integers; Python's arbitrary-precision integers keep going, at the cost of ever-larger multiplications.

use: First recursion lesson: base case, recursive case, call stack, unwinding
Visualising how the call stack grows and unwinds
Small combinatorics (permutations of a handful of items) where exact integers suffice
avoid: Large n: depth exceeds default stack limits and results become astronomically large
Performance-sensitive code — the loop is cheaper in every dimension
Fixed-width integer languages beyond 20! — the result overflows silently

commonMistakes.mistake: Missing or misplaced base case — recursing below 1 forever until the stack overflows.
commonMistakes.fix: Return 1 for n <= 1 before any recursive call.

commonMistakes.mistake: Negative input unhandled: factorial(-3) descends past zero forever in a hand-written version.
commonMistakes.fix: Validate n >= 0 up front, or delegate to math.factorial, which raises ValueError.

commonMistakes.mistake: Expecting exact results past 20! in fixed-width languages, where the multiplication wraps and returns a plausible wrong number.
commonMistakes.fix: Use arbitrary-precision integers (Python, BigInteger in Java, BigInt in JS), or work with logarithms or modular arithmetic when only magnitude or a residue is needed.

name: Tower of Hanoi
description: Move n disks between pegs, one at a time, never placing a larger disk on a smaller one. The optimal solution takes exactly 2^n - 1 moves and is the cleanest illustration of recursive decomposition.
explanation:
What it is

The puzzle: n disks of different sizes stacked on one peg, two empty pegs, and the rules — one disk per move, only the top disk of a peg may move, and a larger disk may never rest on a smaller one. The recursive solution is three lines and provably optimal.

How it works

  1. Move the top n - 1 disks from the source to the auxiliary peg (recursively).
  2. Move the largest disk from source to destination — its only move in the whole solution.
  3. Move the n - 1 disks from auxiliary to destination (recursively).

Worked example

n = 3: move disks 1-2 to the auxiliary peg (3 moves), move disk 3 across, move disks 1-2 to join it (3 moves) — 7 moves total = 2^3 - 1. n = 10: 1023 moves. The count is unavoidable: the largest disk must move at least once, and everything above it must move at least twice.

Key insight

The recurrence T(n) = 2T(n - 1) + 1 with T(0) = 0 solves to exactly 2^n - 1 moves: optimality is part of the structure, not an accident. The lesson generalises the other way too — if a problem decomposes into two independent (n - 1) subproblems like this, expect exponential scale, and look for the shared structure that collapses it. The classic n = 64 version needs about 585 billion years at one move per second.

use: Teaching recursion structure and induction proofs together
Making exponential growth concrete (each extra disk doubles the work)
A warm-up for the divide-and-conquer mindset: reduce to a smaller instance
avoid: Any practical n beyond about 30 — 2^n dominates everything
As a template for problems whose subproblems genuinely overlap; here the exponential part is intrinsic and unremovable

commonMistakes.mistake: Moving the n - 1 stack straight to the destination peg, which blocks the largest disk from ever moving — the rule violation is built into the call arguments.
commonMistakes.fix: The three steps are: (n - 1) from source to auxiliary, largest disk source to destination, (n - 1) from auxiliary to destination.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reporting 2^n or n moves instead of 2^n - 1 — an off-by-one that grows exponentially.
commonMistakes.fix: Prove it from the recurrence: T(n) = 2T(n - 1) + 1, T(0) = 0 gives exactly 2^n - 1.

commonMistakes.mistake: No base case for the smallest disk (or no n = 0 case), so recursion never bottoms out.
commonMistakes.fix: Return immediately for n <= 0; move a single disk when n == 1.
